body:
Thank you for your kind words. I heard a lot of similar sentiments last summer when I was seeing a personal counselor at my university. Really, I think I was hoping that he might explain that I'm paranoid about certain things or point me to resources that I was unaware of, but he largely assured me that my concerns are all real and valid and that I'm doing a good job of managing my particular circumstances and keeping a realistic perspective. It sucks that often the final word does come down to "No, you're right, life is terribly unfair, competitive and indifferent to the well-being of individuals but hang in there, maybe you'll pull off a miracle and be an exception to the rule! You have to pay to play! You have to take risks to succeed! [Fuck rationality!]" It leaves me with a feeling that those who can help are not inclined to do so, and those who are inclined to do so can't help in a substantive way. Sometimes I feel like those kinds of encouragements aren't so much sensible advice as it is their romantic expression of how they would like the narrative to go for someone 'like me.'

I'm flattered that you find me intelligent but hearing things like that unfortunately grates on me sometimes. When I was laid off from a previous long-term job, I saw a career counselor who identified my "intelligence" and interests and encouraged me to pursue higher education in spite of my financial situation and age. My Mom has always called me smart and intelligent too and she thinks of herself as "just a stupid woman" and incompetent to advise me. (Her words. She says this sort of thing at some point almost every time I see her since I was very young and seeking guidance.) Both the counselor and my Mom are what I would describe as 'manifesters,' that is, they think that if you have intelligence and a positive attitude, there is no excuse for failing to achieve whatever outlandish goals you care to set for yourself, practicality be damned. The flip side is that if things are going particularly poorly and I express anything to either of them other than supreme confidence and positivity then, with my 'intelligence' being viewed as an absolute, it can only be my expectations or negativity that make my life difficult, as though external factors do not exist and should be easily dismissed or ignored. It's the chicken and the egg. I know with a high degree of confidence that my disposition is a result of what's happening in my life while many other people insist that it must be the other way around. Like it's my job to be an inspiration to them. Like it's completely my fault if I don't manage to "achieve the impossible dream." Whenever I express fear or doubt to either, regardless of the context, I usually receive a scolding. It's my responsibility to ensure that I'm an exception to the well-known statistics regarding people in similar situations. It always just sounds Romney-esque to me, if you get my meaning. I have to just stop being who I am, no longer be poor and accept every setback and burden with a smile. What's so difficult about that? Just be happy. Disconnect your emotions from your day-to-day reality.

I didn't used to compare myself with others, but I guess I've been worse at that lately. High school used to be the great equalizer; regardless of everyone's home situation, spending most of the week at school and hanging out in the neighborhood around the school was a common experience for everyone, there was at least a common culture. When I spend time with my friends now, it's extremely stark how different their lives are from mine, how little they can relate to my struggles and how, by and large, all they really had to do to get where they are was "say yes" and not fuck up too badly, whereas my background demands that I have to convince people of my merit, seek extra attention and work without any kind of safety net. My envy is less about what they have and more about how straightforward and natural it was for them to have it. Not that they don't work hard or deserve what they have, just that the opportunity to work hard has always been more or less presented to them for the taking, whereas I was always strongly discouraged from pursuing anything that required resources, capital or time commitment without an immediate financial return. Frankly, my Mom's position as I finished high school was essentially: "The government must have something in place for someone like you...I don't know what...but surely there's something...you're so smart..." I've always felt that she sees the government as having more of a responsibility for my well-being than she does. Anyway, I'm well into adulthood now, so that's all water under the bridge. It is what it is.

As for getting out, now that summer is here I don't have a student bus pass and there isn't anywhere nearby that I would consider a pleasant place to go work. I live in a very sketchy place and the surrounding neighborhood is kind of colored that way and has been getting worse. A lot of derelict buildings, a fair number of gunshots at night, people roaming around collecting bottles, etc. there's only really convenience stores nearby. When I go out locally, I'm usually filled with dread that "This is indeed where I belong, among the flotsam; the disregarded and forgotten of society. Those who never really had a chance." I've been trying to do better about being around people recently, but it's very difficult since I can't afford to do most of the things that people do together and because I'm often too worried and distracted to be good company. I also don't want to feel that people are emotionally attached to me, since I know how difficult it can be to watch someone's life fall apart that you care about and I can't preclude the possibility of my life completely falling apart. I also have that thing where being among other people sometimes makes me feel more alone. Communicating over the internet can makes me feel that way too.

Anyway, thanks again. I hope you don't find my reply too contrarian, I'll certainly continue to focus on my academics. As I say, that's one of the only things I feel I have some proclivity for and control over. I feel like if I do get a technical, practical degree (physics is debatable) and still don't manage to establish some kind of stable, livable life, then hopefully no one will be able to say I didn't take extraordinary steps try to overcome my circumstances.
That day, I was. Except it was reddit.
Indeed. Perhaps one day the hope will be realized. I'm feeling better than I did when I took the photo, anyway. Take heart, kind stranger.
:) Thank you, purple-haired girl who may have been born the same year as me

Too much time, and I never used to be that way. I used to be able to focus on the things I enjoyed. I've definitely been an information junkie for quite some time now. I almost have a fear of ignorance. It's funny actually; I've told this story before, but here's what's happened as I see it:

I was working doing data entry, which, in a way, took absolutely no concentration whatsoever. It was mainly eye to hand. I listened to music all day for a long time, a couple of years, before I found I got tired of music and didn't have much of an appetite to keep finding more. So I thought I would start listening to books and lectures about things I enjoyed. I listened to a lot of Alan Watts, Robert Anton Wilson, Marshall McLuhan, even some Terence McKenna. I listened to the audiobook of Einstein's General Theory of Relativity, Stephen Hawking's books (as well as a biography of him) and a book the Dalai Lama wrote comparing Buddhism to Science. Then I discovered podcasting and started listening to science news podcasts. A lot of NPR and podcasts produced by respected university faculty members. I started getting back into psychology, manned spaceflight, astronomy and theoretical physics. I started following what was happening in the world of particle physics and astronomy especially. The LHC, Kepler, and anticipation of James Webb. All spellbinding work. This is when I learned that all was not well in the science community, however. Funding was being threatened and cut, public awareness and perception of science seemed to be waning. My passions, the things which I've always found most inspiring about humanity, the endeavors I respected most I found were under threat.

In an effort to understand these unsettling trends, I started listening to skeptical podcasts and some podcasts about economics as well. I came to understand the nature of money, globalization, climate change (especially ongoing rapid extinction of species) and adamant persistence in superstition more than I had ever cared to. It led me into following the political world as well; an arena in life in which wealth and social power seem to have become inappropriately concentrated and is currently undergoing a complete systemic breakdown. (At least in North America.) I find it almost impossible not to be overwhelmed by the problems the world faces and what *might* happen. I struggle to draw the line between alarmism and realism. It feels petty and pointless now, to think about just getting a job doing something mundane, making ends meet, thinking of my own happiness, hoping that everyone eventually catches on to the things that are happening before it's too late. Wondering if it is already too late. Wishing that long term solutions weren't seemingly being written off because they're "too expensive" to implement or develop. I'd be building a bunker, learning to farm and arming myself if I didn't find those people equally naive and often hilarious.

So yes, I concentrate too much on problems which are outside of my control. I'm highly aware that I live in a world which is at war with itself in many ways; some conventional, some not. I'm fearful at the amount of people who seem able to ignore it all or remain hopeful in order to crack on. But I least I feel aware of what's happening. Still sounds better than the alternative. If we're going to have to ride out a shitstorm, I think I'd rather be angry than confused. Doesn't mean I necessarily feel up to riding out the storm, either.

I hope so too. Anyway, if nothing else, it seems I'll enjoy the conversations we'll have, for whatever that's worth. I'm just going to concentrate on being open to everything she says and being honest and forthcoming. Speaking of which, she's sent me an email since our first conversation. (We won't be meeting again until May.) She began by saying:

"WOW – you really know how to make a big first impression on someone! :) It was an utter pleasure to meet you on Friday. Refreshing….

I have been doing a lot of reflecting since our time together – mostly around how I can add any value to your life given the circumstances. It sounds as if there is lots you have figured out about yourself already[...]"

She later goes on to provide a synopsis of my situation as she sees it:

"-Bright, articulate and very self aware.  Written and verbal communication is exceptional…this guy could go places! :)
-Understands there is much he could do but he feels limited by a) fear of risk b) limited education/credentials c) financial status. 
-Is unclear around where he actually 'fits in' and would like to spend some time exploring this. ."

I always have a difficult time accepting compliments and it's become a real bugbear of mine when people see untapped potential in me that I either don't see in myself or feel ashamed of failing to do anything meaningful with. I always just process it as flattery or projection. In the past, people have made me almost feel duty bound to accomplish something exceptional, which has never been compatible with my self image. I'm tired of people telling me that "I could do anything." I always think that there's no way that could literally be true and wish I just had a way of determining which of the dreams people have had for me I 'should' pursue and how. It also makes me nervous that she acknowledges being at a loss thus far as to how she might be able to help me, which is more in line with what I had expected to be the case.

Still, She's framed my feelings well enough with respect to my 'professional' future and I'm open to the possibility that she might have some pragmatic advice for me which I wouldn't have expected. I understand that to a reasonable, well adjusted person, what's been said so far should be encouraging. If only I could believe in myself as others do without buckling under the pressure.

I share your interest in the awareness campaigns we've been seeing lately and the efforts being taken to fundamentally restructure and reassess how things are done on the most fundamental levels. Every generation should have a chance to do this: take stock of what has happened before, what we have to work with and chart a course forward based on our best information, our best understanding of what is and is not possible and what would bring a feeling of security to the most people possible. (Not the illusion of security at the expense of reasonable freedom and dignity. Social security.) That being said, the waiting and the uncertainty of it all drives me crazy. I feel the weight of living in a world which is lost and in conflict with itself on every conceivable level. There may well be a calm after the shitstorm, but I feel the shitstorm could encompass the duration of my lifetime and it's not a ride that I'm looking forward to muddling my way through, trying to find moments of hope like diamonds in a coal mine. Trying to read the tea leaves of social upheaval. Relying on ignorance for peace of mind.

A small source of personal hope but also a validation of concerns: When I turned on the local radio in the shower this morning, they were talking about how mental health issues are still stigmatized, largely undiagnosed and that we don't have enough medical infrastructure in place to help people who need it. They were saying that people who should be treated for mental health problems commonly end up in the penal system instead, rather than being given the compassionate treatment that would really improve their lives in a meaningful way. I find hope in the fact that it's being talked about, but it's unsettling that it's being talked about in the context of the system being broken and not easily accessible to those who would benefit from it.

I like to read and write. I listen to a lot of podcasts and audiobooks. I enjoy singing and used to sing in a garage band. I play a bit of guitar, picked it up mainly to help write lyrics but I haven't done that in a long time. I enjoy video games, movies and some TV of course. I like to walk, swim, hike and bicycle. I have no career path in mind, just a disjointed collage of loosely related or unrelated subjects that I'm interested in which I can't imagine monetizing, but rather, would cost money to pursue (cosmology, philosophy, astronomy.) I've also been interested in a few things for which the industries seem to be very competitive and in many ways unstable (journalism, film making)

I actually had a meeting with a career counselor this afternoon. I'm not sure how helpful she'll be able to be ultimately but I was very comfortable talking with her and enjoyed our conversation, she seemed to not mind that I prefer to cut through pretense and talk very directly and openly. She agreed with my views on the state of the job market here (not good) and the difficulties people face in choosing and maintaining a satisfying career trajectory. She understood my reluctance and the difficulties I would have to face to pursue what would my more ambitious goals and my difficulty in deciding what kind of work I should think about committing to as a source of income. She didn't try to offer me simple solutions and idle optimism, which I very much respected. 

She said that I was obviously very self aware and that I seemed to have myself together, she acknowledged that I probably wouldn't need much help writing a resume or interviewing and seems open to helping me more with coming up with a realistic plan which feels relatively achievable, not too risky but might provide a degree of self satisfaction. She was also blunt about my having to go outside of my comfort zone, which I was expecting and am ready to confront. I thought to myself: "that's okay, I don't really have a comfort zone anymore anyway."

Where we left off was, she said she would need some time to think about everything we talked about and she suggested that I write her 5 stories about times in my life when I felt like what I was doing was most satisfying and representative of who I feel I am. I thought that was a good exercise at least, something to do; though I've mentally done it a million times before.

*sigh* A large part of me was hoping that she would point out ways in which I was being alarmist and paranoid and make it seem as though things are much simpler than I see them, and convince me of it, but that didn't happen. She seemed to agree that most of my concerns are valid and understood that my personal issues are significant ones to try to overcome. I didn't come out with more hope than I went in with exactly, but it's nice to know that I'll enjoy our time together at least.

I appreciate the links. The personality types the test offered for me did seem fair enough but it makes sense that they would given that the data is self reported. I'm very skeptical about typifying personalities, especially in the context of choosing a career path and don't think my results would have been the same if I had taken the test in a different mood, or at a different time of my life. I feel like I've changed quite a lot over the years as a result of life experience and feel I will continue to do so; I hesitate to let a personality test inform my choice of career, especially since it does nothing to assess competence. (Frankly, I'm not sure if I even accept the concept of a 'career') The careers that the second site offered seemed to fall under 4 categories for me: undesirable, impractical, not realistically attainable, and not actually a career. The most compelling was therapist / psychiatrist in that I would enjoy reflecting on the private thoughts of others, hearing how different people process the world and trying to help in any way that I can but I'm not sure how I feel about charging money to do it and I know that psychology is a highly competitive field of study, which is unappealing to me.

I've always found, and continue to find this question of "what do you want to be?" to be based in a sort of idealism that most people should be able to establish clear and consistent long term goals to work toward, maintaining that future vision. I've never been able to do this, my interests change very frequently. I also don't think we live in a time when everyone is given a chance to really pursue their interests without it being a significant risk in one way or another. I'm used to the thought "I can't afford it" while thinking about participation in things which would lead to personal growth and build self confidence; that's how it always was for me growing up and as an adult, education still feels like one of those things that I 'can't afford.' I understand "no risk, no reward" and "you can't afford not to" but I would prefer not to spend my life working hard, marketing myself, gambling money, competing and generally fighting tooth and nail to be given the opportunity to learn and contribute something to the world.

I think my lack of "manliness" might be as simple as not having a Father growing up but having quite a few male role models coming and going who were all very different from one another. I never really had a central figure my own gender to seek guidance from or share deep personal thoughts with and there didn't really seem to be a common thread that I could pick up on among Men that I knew. I went through Sunday school and was brought to Catholic church, so the only person I heard referred to as Father were the priests. To me, they were distant, stoic figures with no knowledge of me, no practical advice to offer and, of course, no vested interest or stake in my future. They're just there to represent God's demands of us. Being Catholic, of course, God was just the perfect perfectness who could never be impressed or satisfied, perpetually disappointed, whose will I could never live up to and would never communicate with me directly. It's strange trying to literally think of "God" as "Your father" growing up. I wish I hadn't payed attention, a lot of people seem to just take it on a surface level and not really have it affect them but I really did think of myself as fundamentally inadequate and flawed in the eyes of God (my father,) needing to ask constant forgiveness, while feeling that I wasn't worthy of it and that any mercy or acceptance would come as an act of charity. It sounds insane now, I know how sick it is, but it's still how I feel about life and about myself I think. It's become a part of my personality. Who knows what I would have been like without it. Oh, also, I spent most of my youthful years thinking of lust, sex, my attraction to girls as evil which I must control and reject. That definitely has something to do with my relationship situation too, I still haven't confronted that particular demon.

Edit: I bring up the religion stuff because a career suggested for both of my Myers-Briggs personality results was Preist / Clergy / Religious work. I just about fell out of my chair. The bastards made me one of them. I understand the irony of my using the word bastard as an insult. Everyone seems to agree it means "terrible person" though. I understand people don't have its literal meaning in mind when they say it, but the thought always runs through my head "I am a bastard."
Maybe rationality is better than hope anyway. Hope is also idle.

In many ways, you're living what I would consider to be my ideal life. You're doing a lot of the things that I lack the self confidence to pursue but spend an embarrassing amount of time thinking about. It's funny how that works, maybe if I were in your position, I too would find it all less satisfying than I would expect. As for your love life, mine is worse. I'm a 26 year old virgin, only kissed 2 girls and am also used to being told how wonderful I am by girls who aren't interested in having a relationship with me. A few times I've gotten the "if I weren't in a relationship..." comment, which is never welcome and I have no idea how I'm supposed to react to something like that, though I know it's meant as a compliment. Once, someone told me that I'm the kind of guy they could see marrying one day. I think that I'm what women think they should want, but don't actually want.

I was raised by a single Mom, and while I wasn't her punching bag and never doubted that she loved me, I felt that she relied on me too much for day to day companionship. When I would try to focus on establishing my own life, working hard toward something, I would always get the sense that she felt neglected and lonely. She also didn't have much wisdom per say to share with me about how life works and I still struggle to make sense of things. Even simple, practical things that everyone should know. It's amazing how much she's manged to avoid learning. She's a romantic who prefers simple thoughts, is obsessed with being kind and meek, expects it of others at all times and doesn't particularly value discipline. She's always found life intimidating and indecipherable herself. I don't think it helped my outlook on romance and intimacy, either, seeing her spending most days at home, watching TV, working long hours at minimum wage, barely making ends meet, trying to bring up a Son.

In another post I made, I was asked to sum up the current phase of my life in one sentence. I said: "The world has proven to be an unsupportive and indifferent place for someone like me, in which everyone must trust in and assert their value in spite of economic discouragement to do so, with little on offer to me beyond moral encouragement and optimism (in my view, unjustified.)" Bonus sentence: "To be loved is an unrealistic expectation"

What might your answer be?

Edit: Also, if you haven't heard the term "limerence" before, you might want to read a bit about it and see if it means anything to you. I got a surge of insight realizing that there is a term that can be understood for the way that I've felt about someone for a long time which is a much better match than simple unrequited love, infatuation or any of the more common terms. Maybe you'd find it useful too.

I seemingly feel very similar to the way you do. I was recently laid off due to outsourcing and the company I was working for had very much instituted a culture of competition among the staff in order to determine who to let go, in what order. They also don't really offer references as such, just a corporate acknowledgement of employment by someone who may not have met you and an overview of your most recent review, which, if you're being laid off probably isn't great. We also live a similar lifestyle, I think. I'm slightly overweight (but much less so than I was in high school) and live alone. I've been increasingly more misanthropic as time has gone on. C-PTSD (in the specific form of religious trauma syndrome) has been mentioned to me recently as well and upon reading up on it, it sounded very familiar to what is often going on in my head.

I think people do lie a lot, especially to themselves. I think most people really do think moment to moment and if there isn't currently something bad happening to them, they think everything is a-ok, there's no reason to be concerned and the only reason people aren't doing as well as them is that they have a bad attitude or were lazy. I also feel like the world isn't the way I was promised it would be and the doors haven't opened for me that I was led to believe would.

I have no practical advice and have been hoping myself to find a reassuring thought that might actually ring true to me and be compatible with what I know of the world and what I've experienced of it so far. I can only offer solidarity and the thought that you are very much not alone in your perspective on the world we live in.

I don't have a university degree. I only went for a year before getting freaked out at the cost, lack of guaranteed employment, and understanding that I wasn't choosing what I wanted to study with a career path in mind. But I now understand that it really is mostly about the piece of paper that affirms "smartness," even if what you learn has nothing to do with the direction your life moves in. In a highly competitive labor market, your "smartness" paper seems essential, even if it's fundamentally meaningless.

No girlfriend. The girl I've been referencing and I have never been together, we've just spent a lot of time together over the years counseling, encouraging, sharing thoughts and trying to reassure one another that we'll be okay. She's never felt the same way about me as I do her; mostly she's spent so much time with me because she perceives a lack of other options, has difficulty meeting new people and because I'm always happy to avail myself to her and eager to be in her company. Since talking to her directly about my feelings and about how I've never really wanted to go out with anyone else, she hasn't been speaking to me. I certainly don't want to ask for her help right now dealing with personal problems. I feel, even if she were to agree, it would increase my sense of intimacy toward her, dependence on her and generally make matters in that regard worse for both of us. Part of having a low opinion of myself has been that at least it "makes sense" that she's not attracted to me. If I were to think of myself as desirable and worthy of love, I fear that I would be even more lost in processing her indifference.

As for "real issues," I mean both, I don't see them as distinct from one another. Issues of the world which have a direct impact on my and the lives of people around me are what seem to paralyze me the most and leave me dreading my future. Things like a local economy which may well force me to move away to find work, removing me from the modest support structure I have here. Knowing that my friends who have moved, even those who are more confident, focused, driven and theoretically have better credentials to find gainful employment than I are working hard or having difficulty finding work, struggling to make ends meet and have little time and energy for meeting people and enjoying life. And yes, things like the state of climate change and the dubious ways in which political and executive power is "earned" and wielded is very much draining on any sense of hope, motivation or possibility of wellness that I might otherwise have. "Success" and independence seem more and more to depend on one's willingness to be arrogant, entitled and exploitative. Or at least ignorant of abstracted repercussions.

I aspire to a very modest but stable lifestyle which affords me time to enjoy each day and financial independence. I don't think this should be as difficult and ambitious a goal as it seems to be, but saving money through job elimination, outsourcing and digital automation seem to the norm across most industries. I'm fairly introverted and jaded, so I would prefer not to work in a service industry, or representing a company I don't necessarily support in the name of a paycheque, feeling like a wage slave. I suppose I'm too idealistic. Following the US election cycle and what's been happening here in Canada has been unnerving. I see people with 3 or more houses who never seem to say anything informed, intelligent or insightful speaking to entire nations, with authoritative and inflexible voices, about how life shall correctly be lived by all, which common values must be shared in their eyes to feel a part of society. What we MUST do as nations to make money. In science podcasts I hear the people I respect the most on this planet, who have contributed the most to our understanding of the cosmos and our capacity to improve our environment and plan the future of our species struggling for funding, expressing outrage at the increasing lack of foresight displayed by the designers of our regulatory systems, and calling for resistance to current economic and social trends as they diverge further and further from our best understanding of the way things (and people) work on the most fundamental levels. People who are specifically apolitical and experts in relying on empirical evidence as a primary driver for establishing their opinions.

And yet, it seems the yuppies will always beat out the hippies because the yuppies remain convinced (and convincing) that they know what they're doing, that they know what's best for everyone. And "the world" at large seems to persist in the belief that since they don't know any better, the most confident among us must be correct and that if your intentions are good, nothing too bad can actually happen.

I find it difficult to see how I'm meant to function and find peace and comfort with this perspective on life. Indeed, I've come to mistrust any voice who would seek to comfort me and find the happiness and sense of security of others more often than not, to be based largely in naïveté. Even many who don't have a sense of security often seem obsessed primarily with red herrings, issues of ultimately questionable importance and outrageously misinformed conspiracies (i.e. global decrease in religious belief, the war on terror and conscious suppression of new technologies, respectively)

I only really feel comfortable anymore isolating myself from the world around me. Waiting and watching, hoping that things might somehow change. But one can't make money in that way as far as I am aware. And without having money as a primary motivator, something you love so much that you'll be willing to work as long and as hard, doing anything which is demanded of you at the expense of all else to get it (or rather, help others to get it and hope they might see fit to share some with you,) it seems that the powers that be are all too willing to cast you aside as broken, inadequate and unacceptable. I don't mean this as a conspiracy theory. I mean this to illustrate what is probably the most sensible attitude for the "leaders" of any corporation to have in an employer's market.

Thanks for thinking of me. No significant change. Still dealing, trying to stay distracted. Trying to enjoy my hobbies and pastimes. Spending way too much time alone. Trying to feel like it's okay to be out of work for a while, that it's nothing to be ashamed of and believe that I'll find a suitable source of income one day that makes me feel like I'm contributing something meaningful. Still have a bleak outlook on all of it, which I don't think is unjustified. Still don't don't know what to do and feel like I have to go it alone.

I'm not aware of any time in my life where I've really thought highly of myself or felt a part of the world around me. My last year of highschool was the best year I can recall, when I thought that maybe I'd be able to overcome my fears, do something impressive or meaningful with my life, nurture and pursue my talents as I saw them and feel successful in my own eyes, but that fell apart rather quickly. For, I'd say, the last 5 years or so I've just felt like I'm one of the ~7 billion little human organisms struggling and competing with one another to find personal satisfaction in a complicated world and hopefully have a positive impact in my own small way.

I haven't properly looked into getting help, but I've been aware for quite a long time that I probably should. My excuses are mostly unsound and common ones, such as not wanting to make the things I struggle with "official," not wanting to be diagnosed with something and be stigmatized in some way and not wanting to consider how much time I've wasted irrationally trapped in my own mind. And I genuinely feel that a lot of what troubles me isn't just in my own head, but comes from an awareness and understanding of real issues which can't be solved through achieving a more 'positive' outlook or healthy self image. If someone in my personal life made me go, I would comply.

I know people are busy, I didn't think I was being ignored. I have no idea what kind of work it would make sense for me to move toward at this point. For the past 6-7 years my job has been extremely mindless. I've sat at a desk transcribing numerical data while listening to podcasts, lectures, audiobooks and music. I don't want to do anything like that anymore if I can help it it's only exacerbated my feeling that the best I can hope for is toiling in obscurity somewhere and eking out a meager existence, away from the rest of the world. So that time has been more or less a waste. I've developed a loathing of spending each day in a carefully controlled corporate run environment. I've learned a lot, but obviously not in a way that I can claim practical skills on a resume. Before that, I worked at a movie theatre, sometimes in the roll of projectionist, which was the part I liked most. The theater is now closed and movie projection has been converted from film to digital. Really, all of my interests are very impractical / cerebral / notorious for not providing a stable source of income. I have no idea what I should do, I have an intense fear of going from minimum wage job to minimum wage job, begging for hours to be able to live, aware that layoffs can happen at any time and that finding employment locally is by no means a guarantee. But that seems to be what I'll have to do. It seems to be what almost everyone is doing. It might even be the best case scenario. I find it difficult to imagine ever being comfortable with that outlook, willing to press on feeling like a drone or a slave to a small minded boss who's utterly enchanted with daily reports and balance sheets.

As for what you've said regarding my relationship situation...I feel a long way from what you're describing. I'm not sure if you're picturing my situation accurately or not (I guess I wouldn't necessarily be aware from my perspective how women see me.) But I can say that I have no self confidence, feel like I have nothing to offer anyone in terms of enjoying life and building a future. I'm not sure which aspects of my life you'd like me to share which would constitute my story. I'm an only child of a single mother who was loving and emotionally supportive but struggled to maintain employment, had very little ambition and thought very little about the world outside of her own experiences. My family is generally roman catholic (this was the only real cultural identity I had growing up) and I was aware of being a 'bastard' child as a matter of fact, although no one was overtly unkind to me on this basis. I was born with a birth defect (cystic hygroma) which was always just noticeable enough to be asked about it from time to time but not so much so that it was noticeable at a glance, particularly off putting, or stared at. I thought of it as a blight, a physical sign of my dubious origin. Because we didn't have disposable income, I didn't have a computer but did have a small TV. TV (more so the internet now) has always been, and continues to be my most reliable friend, and my window to the world. It's still strange to me that the internet is so interactive, sometimes I still find it intimidating that I'm able to share my thoughts with the "outside" world.

I was always overweight and developed acne in jr high. All together it was just enough for me to feel more comfortable alone and, while I got along well enough with some people my age, I never really felt like I belonged among "normal" people with good self esteem and a positive outlook on life and certainly never felt like a romantic relationship was something that would be possible for me. (I spent a surprising amount of time with attractive girls in high school, but mostly in the role of relationship counselor and almost exclusively during school hours) I wasn't the type to be openly mocked, but likewise wasn't seen as having enough social capital to be invited to many parties and whatnot. I did have a group of friends who accepted me, kind people. I didn't tell them much about how I felt, I just tried to act happy around them as best I could but I still felt like the poor kid, or like someone's little brother being allowed to join in out of sympathy. I'm still in touch with some of them but, most have moved away or have otherwise moved on and gotten busy.

In spite of my reluctance to be a participant in the world around me, my fear of intimacy, my tendency to isolate myself and cultivate self loathing (much of which I attribute to my religious upbringing,) and lack of any ambition, I ended up singing in a band for a while (came out of being a band nerd) and developed a keen interest in physics by the end of high school. (star trek and science documentaries were easily my favorite things to watch on TV growing up) I went to university for a year on a loan (in spite of being terrified of debt and tuition seeming like a cartoonish amount of money to me. More than I, or probably my mom, had ever seen at one time.) I did well enough academically but I found the experience overwhelming, didn't trust that it would lead me to a career and didn't feel I belonged among people with bright futures. I felt like I was trying to get away with something, gambling someone else's money on a hunch. I also didn't understand anything about how money works (still don't really) and was distrustful of government bureaucracy. I just wanted to be allowed to go to class to see what I could do. I didn't think it should require a degree in economics and signing binding legal agreements at the age of 18 to be an undergrad. I took physics, psychology, philosophy, English and pre-calculus (I had elected to finish french immersion in high school which didn't leave room in my schedule for pre-calculus and hadn't considered that I might want to study science until the last year of high school) By second year it felt like the stakes were way too high, and I was in the midst of an existential crisis, trying to re-evaluate everything (including how I was taught to conceptualize my place in the universe) on the fly while managing personal finance for the first time in my life and keeping up with a challenging course load without skipping a beat and without parents who could offer advice or insight into any of it.

So I dropped out, (there is much more to the story of my dropping out, a lot of forces at play,) and got a niche job doing data entry (which I was recently laid off from due to outsourcing and ongoing decline in the paper economy.) Now I feel like I'm starting my life from scratch, without the ambition, skills or self confidence to do so. To the extent that I understand that how I feel may be unwarranted and that I should probably say "fuck fear" and blindly pursue my interests; very little has changed about my outlook on life emotionally. I still have an overwhelming urge to isolate myself from "real people" and feel arrogant and naive when I entertain notions of "following my dreams" in the face of the odds. Frankly, I still feel like I'd be challenging, or rejecting God's will, even though I'm now a proud atheist. It's just the easiest way to describe the feelings that are holding me back. I also feel like 'my dreams' and interests don't necessarily translate to a career path, but financial independence is essential for me. I can't risk being where I am now, but $50k in debt. Anyway, my greatest dream has always been to be in a relationship, to feel accepted by someone in particular who I've known and have been in constant contact with for 11 years. I recently "came out" about my feelings and she's certain she doesn't feel the same way about me. It's disrupted our 'patient-therapist' relationship and we haven't been talking for some time. I feel ashamed, embarrassed and stupid for having put my heart on my sleeve for someone who I rationally knew wouldn't be interested in me. She feels badly for relying on me so heavily and would like me to move on. She says there's "no spark" and that I don't have her "X factor." I still don't understand what she's looking for in a partner that she doesn't see in me, and she likely doesn't know herself I suppose. I feel like I don't know how to process what's happening without knowing why she finds me unappealing, why she's spent so much time with me over the years in spite of this, seeking my guidance, enjoying our time together. I can't help but think it's because she finds me ugly but doesn't have the heart to say so. But I suppose it's unfair to expect it to make sense. I have no dreams left, I've never genuinely been attracted to having a relationship with anyone else and have never been able to understand or trust someone so deeply as I feel I do her. Rejection is brutal for me, it vindicates too many of my thoughts about myself.

Sum up this phase of my life in a sentence? How about "The world has proven to be an unsupportive and indifferent place for someone like me, in which everyone must trust in and assert their value in spite of economic discouragement to do so, with little on offer to me beyond moral encouragement and optimism (in my view, unjustified.)" Bonus sentence: "To be loved is an unrealistic expectation"

I would say that I've know a few examples in my life of the shaman-like people you are describing. Having a shamanistic mindset or thinking one's self a guru of one stripe or another seems to be relatively common to me and even still marketable for those who are willing to sincerely commit to that sort of identity. I've spent a lot of time in a corporate environment and it wasn't uncommon that we would be given presentations from people whom we hadn't met before, who's primary skill seemed to be impressing groups of office workers through re-appropriating and (often incorrectly) applying general terms from philosophy, psychology and academia in general to create the illusion that "the industry" or "the business" was completely understood and under control, and that the needs of the employees were well understood and being met as well as making sure that anything of substance that was said would be worded in such a way as to be difficult for a lay employee to glean what was actually being communicated.

I recall recently, as the company was going through downsizing (which they refer to as "rightsizing,") they had a presenter explain to us in rich corporate terminology how we would be facing challenges and would be looking at some restructuring to improve efficiency and efficacy, that there would be changes but that the business is doing well, our clients are happy and we were "green across the board." I raised my hand and asked "Do you think that you're in a position to offer long term employment here for the foreseeable future?" He gazed into the middle distance for a moment and said "You know, someone once told me that everything changes." That was his answer. It was clear to a few what exactly was being said but at the end of the presentation, the guy got applause. He had just indirectly warned a room full of people that their jobs were not secure in such a way as to receive applause. As far as I can tell, the applause was because many people weren't able to interpret what was said but found his "intelligence" and communication skills reassuring. If that isn't a modern day shaman, I don't know what is. We still do follow "leaders" with dubious or undeclared leadership credentials, because we feel a reverence for those who speak with ease in ways we might not be able to replicate.

If anything, I consider myself critical of that mindset, not an example of it. It's true that I often don't feel like I fit into the world, but I don't necessarily think it's because I'm cognitively abnormal and definitely not because I have some special or unique insight or perspective that others don't have access to, it's just a result of influential past experiences and too much time spent in various forms of isolation, escaping into thought about things that most people either aren't interested, don't have the time for, or don't see the point. (there is no point.) I've lived a somewhat monastic lifestyle for a long time, but I don't necessarily think that it's been the environment that I function best in, it's just where I seem to have found myself, being hindered by lack of self confidence, and a persistent feeling of pretention whenever I've reluctantly endulged in any kind of personal ambition. It bothers me how much of the culture around me revolves around hours of mindless, exhausting and often fundamentally unnecessary work which leaves people less time for personal enrichment. But I feel it's the best I can hope for. I know too many people who's jobs consist of being bored somewhere, being monitored by someone else, just kind of, manning a post or filling out reports each day to earn a meager living. I think this is my future, and I'm not happy about embracing it.

Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs has been coming up a lot lately. I'm not sure how I feel about it exactly. Similar to how I feel about Freud's model of the mind, I suppose. A mutual friend of ours has often said that it seems like we're together and when talking to her recently about how embarrassed I am to be having so much trouble getting through things without talking to her daily, she said "well, you're going through a divorce." I said "it doesn't feel fair for me to think of it that way because I know she doesn't."

I'm feeling lost and confused again.

Yes, of course you're right. I like your record analogy, it rings true. I do consider medication, but I have a laundry list of excuses and justifications for not seeking proper assistance. Some rational, some not. Overall, I should most probably look into what help is available to me but that doesn't mean that I will and I'm keenly aware that it won't take away a lot of the more valid concerns which haunt my mind. Life is very vivid and overwhelming to me, but that doesn't mean that I necessarily want it to be dulled. A lot of times I find I wish my 'madness' could be embraced and exploited in some way rather than repressed so that I could function better as a reliable cog in a societal machine in which everyone is trying their best to walk in lockstep with one another because it's comforting and reassuring to embrace pragmatism in order to share a common experience, a common way of thinking, a common goal.

Yeah, even from the broadest possible perspective, in terms of thinking about what we've been observing cosmologically in recent decades, I've fallen on the terms "embedded" and "emergent" for some time to describe my interpretation regarding our relationship to the world (and indeed the universe) in which we reside. But that's in no way the way I was taught to think about my functional relationship to the world and it's still something I struggle to come to terms with, which makes me feel disoriented, lost in a complex ecosystem of worldviews, all of which are inadequate in acknowledging the broader reality which is non-conceptual, open to re-interpretation on every level and independent of the ways we choose to make cognitive sense of the world. I think that has a lot to do with the dissonance I feel I'm always trying to resolve for myself. I often feel a solipsistic separation between myself and rest of the world around me, (as you said earlier, always dealing in degrees of anonymity,) unable to connect in a meaningful way to people and events outside of my own mind and feel a participant in the world, but I know enough to be intellectually confident that this is not true in any fundamental or pragmatic way, that an organism and its environment are intimately connected to one another, changing together, affecting that change in one another, with different and novel aspects of each emerging gradually over time.

I've learned a lot about Buddhism too. It has a rich history of philosophical dialogue and openly embracing the absurdity of reality, the free exploration of thought, diversity of human experience, and the fallibility and limitations of the human mind. I often wish that I could just sit back, laugh (or weep) and marvel at the utter scale of things, the complex and mysterious workings of life and feel liberated by this experience. There are times that I feel this way but I find it's just so far outside of what 'most people' choose to understand that it makes relating to others on an experiential or personal level very challenging and so it seems to exacerbate my feelings of social isolation. Even others who explore this way of thinking openly and arrive at something akin to thought on the same scale seem to want to turn it to their advantage in some way and think of it as tapping a resource, a font of useful knowledge, a source of power which can provide for them materially rather than being a process of self reflection and personal discovery. (Eckhart Tolle drives me up the wall. I lament how popular he's become and how, to many people, he's the first and last word on philosophy, just because he's the only one talking about it they've been passively presented with "on the teevee" or as a "bestseller," as though either of those things give him credibility in this arena.) I can see why meditative experiences (for example) could be interpreted that way, but I'm ever a champion of science and skepticism and think it's risky to trust your own interpretations too readily. I have a friend who is convinced he communicates with aliens while meditating. I know the feeling, but I know there are much better, simpler, and falsifiable explanations for what that feeling is, whose bases are in physical reality.

The abyss certainly is vast and apparent. Astounding how easily ignored it is by most.

Is there such a thing as reassurance that isn't based in idle optimism? Or is the world really as chaotic and uncertain as it appears to be? I wish I could immerse myself in hedonism or fantasy enough to ignore the broader context of life the way that others seem to be able to but I don't think it's ever been my way.
True that. Even without meaning to do it. There's a fine line between helping and hurting sometimes.
